paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Fremont, Ohio, was the departure of about two dozen Black men and their families from Fremont, Sandusky County, in May 1903, after striking workers of the Clauss Shear Works stormed a Black family's house on the night of May 11. It followed the killing of a striker, Otto Mischke, in a clash involving Black workers hired to replace the strikers, and those who left included long-time residents as well as strikebreakers. Mobs stoned the homes of Black men in Fremont again on May 19.

Workers at the Clauss Shear Works were on strike in the spring of 1903, and the employers brought in Black workers and Italians to take their places. One of the Black workers, Wheeler Kimbro, had been shot at five times since coming to Fremont, according to a Norwalk dispatch. On the night of Saturday, May 9, Mischke was fatally shot, and Kimbro, Walter Stratton and Lorenzo Martin, all Black, were arrested. A crowd surrounded the jail calling for the prisoners until Sheriff Mason threatened to shoot the first man who tried to break in, and the three were taken to Norwalk.

By the afternoon of May 11, a Norwalk dispatch reported, many Black men, women and children had passed through Norwalk from Fremont bound for Oberlin, among them long-time Fremont residents. That night, according to a Fremont dispatch in the New York Sun, the strikers stormed the house of a Black family; the report named neither the family nor any injuries. The Sun and the Perrysburg Journal put the number who left 'for fear of harm' at two dozen men with their wives and families, nearly all going to Oberlin.

A Columbus dispatch of May 13 said the unionists had ordered the Black strikebreakers to leave Fremont and that the police seemed powerless to protect them. Mayor Engler asked Governor Nash for troops on May 12, but the governor refused, holding that local authorities still had control. By May 13 the town was described as quiet, and about 500 union men escorted Mischke's funeral.

Kimbro, Martin and Stratton were bound over without bail for first-degree murder and indicted by the Sandusky County grand jury. No arrests for the storming of the house or for driving out the Black workers appear in the coverage.

Attacks resumed a week later: a Scripps-McRae telegram reported that 'a large mob of men and boys' stoned the home of Charles Kemp, said to have helped bring in the Black workers, and that his family fled to Clyde. Another dispatch said John Dixon, a Black worker who had not struck, was driven out after his home was stoned, while his wife and children took refuge in the jail.
In June the Jewett Anti-Lynching League in Cleveland collected a little over $21 toward investigating the cases of the three jailed men.

White papers carried the flight as brief wire items, the Sun under the headline 'Negroes Flee Strike Violence.' The Stark County Democrat set it inside a story about the governor's refusal to send troops, noting that the Black and Italian workers' lives were in danger. The Kemp dispatch described the imported workers as men 'some of whom murdered Otto Mischke,' and the Dixon story ran in the Indianapolis Journal, the Rock Island Argus and the Willmar Tribune.

The Cleveland Gazette headed its account 'The Fremont Riot,' wrote that 'it is about time for the truth to have a hearing,' and presented the jailed men as victims of a strikers' mob. Two weeks later it argued that they had defended their lives and faced prejudice throughout Fremont and Sandusky County. The St. Paul Appeal reprinted the Dixon story without his name, while neither Black paper reported the May 11 storming of the house itself.

Accounts of the precipitating shooting differ: a Fremont report in the Courier-Journal said Black men offended by a white woman's question fired the shot, while the Gazette described a mob attack answered in self-defense. The May 19 stoning appears under two names, Kemp and Dixon, and the coverage does not show whether these were one attack or two.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Fremont, Ohio
bases: The papers report about two dozen Black men and their families leaving Fremont for fear of harm after strikers stormed a Black family's house and unionists ordered the Black strikebreakers out of town (A3, A4, A5, A6).

The flight to Oberlin is reported in the Sun and Perrysburg Journal (A3, A5) and independently in a Norwalk dispatch reprinted by the Cleveland Gazette (A6), and the order to leave in a Columbus dispatch (A4); the storming of the house itself rests on the Sun alone (A3).

accounts.label: Fremont wire report
accounts.gist: Strikers stormed the house of a Black family on the night of May 11, and two dozen Black men with their families left for fear of harm, nearly all for Oberlin.

accounts.label: Columbus dispatch
accounts.gist: Unionists ordered the Black strikebreakers to leave Fremont, the police seemed powerless to protect them, and the governor refused troops.

accounts.label: Norwalk dispatch
accounts.gist: A large number of Black men, women and children, including long-time Fremont residents, passed through Norwalk bound for Oberlin and other places.

accounts.label: Black correspondent (Cleveland Gazette)
accounts.gist: A mob of strikers and sympathizers assaulted three Black workers, who fired in self-defense; the three were then nearly lynched.

accounts.label: Fremont wire report on the shooting
accounts.gist: Black men in the street, offended by a question from Mrs. Albert Gommell, fired a shot that struck Mischke at the door of her house.

framing.detail: The Sun headed the item 'Negroes Flee Strike Violence'; the Perrysburg Journal ran it in a 'Buckeye Pickups' column beside Mischke's funeral.
The Stark County Democrat treated the expulsion as a problem of state troops and public order, saying the lives of the Black and Italian workers were in danger.
The Kemp dispatch reported the stoning while describing the imported Black workers as men 'some of whom murdered Otto Mischke.'
The Cleveland Gazette's 'The Fremont Riot' blamed a mob of strikers and sympathizers, and later wrote of prejudice against the jailed men throughout Fremont and Sandusky County.
The St. Paul Appeal reprinted the Dixon story without his name among items on the hardships of Black Americans.

conflicts.note: The white version is a Fremont wire report; the Gazette's is a Black-press account sympathetic to the accused. Neither is sworn testimony.

versions.value: Charles Kemp, who fled with his family to Clyde
John Dixon, who escaped to Norwalk while his wife and children went to the jail

conflicts.note: Both dispatches are dated May 20 and describe a mob stoning a Black man's home the night before; the coverage does not show whether these were one attack or two.
